blocks.content: Paging divides a program into equal pieces without asking whether those pieces mean anything. Segmentation takes the opposite approach: it divides a program logical address space into pieces that actually mean something, a code segment, a data segment, a stack segment, and a heap segment, each sized to fit exactly what it holds.

This chapter builds directly on what you already know about paging. We will look at how segmentation organizes memory around a program real structure instead of arbitrary fixed size chunks, how the segment table tracks each segment base and limit, how a logical address is translated to a physical one with a full worked example, and how segmentation compares to paging across fragmentation, protection, and alignment with program structure. We will also cover segmented paging, the hybrid most real systems actually use.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863902-965990602.png
1. The Core Idea of Segmentation

Paging solves memory allocation by chopping both physical memory and a program logical address space into fixed size pieces called pages and frames. This is mechanically simple and highly effective against fragmentation, but it is also blind. A page boundary falls wherever the fixed size lands, with no regard for whether it splits a function in half, cuts through an array, or lands cleanly between two unrelated parts of a program. Paging does not know or care what a program logical structure looks like.

Segmentation flips this around. Instead of asking how many fixed size chunks a program needs, it asks what the program actually consists of. Most programs are naturally made up of a handful of logical units, and segmentation gives each of these its own segment in the logical address space, sized exactly to what it needs, rather than forcing them into a sequence of uniform pages.
Segments as logical units

["Code segment: holds the program compiled instructions.","Data segment: holds global and static variables.","Stack segment: holds local variables and function call frames.","Heap segment: holds memory allocated dynamically while the program runs."]
items: Code segment: holds the program compiled instructions.
Data segment: holds global and static variables.
Stack segment: holds local variables and function call frames.
Heap segment: holds memory allocated dynamically while the program runs.

blocks.content: Because each segment corresponds to a real part of the program, segments are rarely the same size as one another. A small utility program might have a tiny code segment and barely any heap, while a large in memory application might have a huge heap segment and a comparatively small code segment. Segmentation embraces this variability directly, letting each segment grow or shrink to match the logical unit it represents, instead of stretching a one size fits all page across everything.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Segmentation divides a program into variable sized, logically meaningful segments such as code, data, stack, and heap, instead of dividing it into fixed size pages that ignore the program structure.
2. The Segment Table

Paging needs a page table to remember which frame each page lives in. Segmentation needs an analogous structure called the segment table, but what it stores is different because a segment is not a fixed size. A page table entry only needs to record a frame number, since every frame is the same size and a page always fits exactly into one frame. A segment table entry cannot get away with that, because segments are different sizes, so each entry has to record both where the segment starts and how big it is.

Every entry in the segment table stores two fields. The base is the starting physical address where that segment has been placed in memory. The limit is the length of the segment, meaning how many bytes it occupies. Together, base and limit describe exactly which region of physical memory belongs to that segment, in the same way a page table entry describes exactly which frame a page has been placed into, just with an added length because that length is no longer fixed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863903-102517047.png
A concrete segment table

Consider a small program with four segments: code, data, stack, and heap. When the operating system loads this program, it finds room for each segment somewhere in physical memory and records the result in the segment table shown below. Notice how differently sized each segment is, and how the base addresses do not need to sit next to each other at all.

blocks.title: Base and limit versus frame number
blocks.content: This is the detail that trips people up. A page table entry only ever needs a frame number, because a page size is fixed and known in advance for the whole system. A segment table entry needs both a base and a limit, because segments are different sizes and the hardware has no way to know how big segment 2 is unless the table tells it.
3. Address Translation Step by Step

A logical address under segmentation is not a single plain number. It is split into two parts, a segment number, which says which segment this address falls inside, and an offset, which says how far into that segment the address points. This is similar in spirit to how paging splits a logical address into a page number and a page offset, except the offset here is measured against a segment real limit instead of a fixed page size.

Translating this into a physical address happens in three steps. First, the segment number is used to look up that segment entry in the segment table, retrieving its base and limit. Second, the offset is compared against the limit. If the offset is greater than or equal to the limit, the address falls outside the segment entirely, meaning the program is trying to touch memory it was never given, and the hardware traps this as an illegal access, typically raising a segmentation fault. If the offset is within the limit, the third step simply adds the offset to the base to get the final physical address.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864288-536369013.png

blocks.title: The limit check is a protection mechanism
blocks.content: That comparison between offset and limit is not just bookkeeping, it is what stops one segment from reading or corrupting another. Because the check happens on every single memory access, a program simply cannot construct an address that reaches outside its own segment, no matter what value it computes.
A worked example

Using the segment table from the previous section, suppose a running program generates the logical address segment 1, offset 150. This means the address points 150 bytes into the data segment. The segment table says segment 1, the data segment, has a base of 2000 and a limit of 400. Since 150 is less than 400, the offset is legal, so the physical address is computed as base plus offset, which is 2000 plus 150, giving 2150.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864290-729350944.png

Now compare that with a logical address of segment 1, offset 450. The same segment table entry applies, base 2000 and limit 400, but this time 450 is not less than 400. The offset exceeds the limit, so the hardware refuses to compute a physical address at all and instead traps into the operating system, which will typically terminate the process with a segmentation fault. This is exactly what stops a program from wandering past the end of its own data segment into memory it does not own.
4. Segmentation Versus Paging, A Direct Comparison
blocks.text: 4. Segmentation Versus Paging, A Direct Comparison

blocks.content: With both approaches now on the table, it is worth setting them side by side directly. Paging and segmentation solve the same underlying problem, giving a program the illusion of its own private memory, but they make very different choices about how to slice that memory up, and those choices ripple outward into fragmentation, protection, and how naturally the scheme fits a program real structure.

{"headers":["Dimension","Paging","Segmentation"],"rows":[["Unit size","Fixed size pages, identical for every page in the system","Variable sized segments, each sized to match the logical unit it represents"],["Fragmentation","Internal fragmentation, wasted space inside a partially filled page","External fragmentation, wasted space in scattered holes between segments"],["Alignment with program structure","Purely mechanical, a page boundary has no relationship to the program logical divisions","Naturally aligned, segments map directly onto code, data, stack, and heap"],["Protection granularity","Uniform, every page gets the same kind of protection bits regardless of what it contains","Natural, permissions can be set per logical unit, such as a code segment that is read only and execute only"]]}

The protection difference is worth dwelling on. Because a page is a fixed size slice with no awareness of what it holds, a single page can easily straddle the boundary between two logically different things, such as the tail end of code and the start of data, forcing the operating system to give that whole page the same permissions even though only part of it should really be executable. A segment, by contrast, is defined to exactly match one logical unit, so marking the entire code segment as read only and execute only, or the entire stack segment as readable and writable but never executable, is both natural and precise.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864290-505396926.png
blocks.alt: Segmentation Versus Paging, A Direct Comparison

blocks.content: Where they agree

It is easy to focus only on the differences, but paging and segmentation are solving the exact same problem underneath, giving each process the illusion of a private, contiguous address space while the operating system actually scatters things around physical memory however it needs to. Both rely on a lookup table maintained by the operating system and consulted by hardware on every memory access, and both add a check that prevents a process from touching memory outside what it has been given. The real difference is the unit being managed, uniform pages in one case, meaningful variable sized segments in the other.
5. Why External Fragmentation Returns

One of paging biggest selling points is that it eliminates external fragmentation almost entirely, since every free frame is exactly the same size and can hold any page. Segmentation gives that benefit up. Because segments are variable sized, just like the contiguous allocations discussed in the Memory Allocation and Fragmentation topics, finding room for a new segment means finding a single contiguous hole in physical memory that is large enough to fit it, not just any collection of free space.

As segments are created and destroyed over the life of a system, physical memory fills up with a scattering of free holes of different sizes, wedged between the segments that are still in use. A new segment might fail to find room even when the total free memory across all the holes would easily be enough, simply because no single hole is big enough on its own. This is precisely the external fragmentation problem, and it is the same failure mode that contiguous memory allocation runs into, for the same underlying reason, variable sized regions competing for variable sized gaps.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864291-224833728.png
Compaction as a partial fix

The classic response to external fragmentation is compaction, physically shifting segments in memory to squeeze all the free space together into one large usable block. This works, but it is expensive, since it means pausing processes and copying potentially large amounts of memory, and it has to be repeated as fragmentation builds back up over time. It treats the symptom rather than removing the underlying cause, which is that segments, unlike pages, do not come in one convenient uniform size.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864291-92750750.png
6. Segmented Paging, A Real World Hybrid
blocks.text: 6. Segmented Paging, A Real World Hybrid

blocks.content: Given that segmentation offers meaningful, protection friendly structure but suffers external fragmentation, while paging offers fragmentation resistance but no structural meaning, a natural question is whether a system can get both. Many practical systems answer yes, using a hybrid called segmented paging. The idea is straightforward, keep the logical division into segments such as code, data, stack, and heap, but instead of allocating each segment as one contiguous block of physical memory, divide every segment internally into fixed size pages.

Under segmented paging, a logical address still starts with a segment number, exactly as in pure segmentation. But instead of that segment number pointing directly to a base and limit in physical memory, it points to a page table that belongs to that specific segment. The offset within the segment is then further split into a page number and a page offset, and that segment own page table is used to translate the page number into a physical frame, exactly like ordinary paging, just scoped to one segment at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864291-602952803.png
blocks.alt: Segmented Paging, A Real World Hybrid

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Fragmentation","Structure"],"rows":[["Pure segmentation","External fragmentation between segments","Strong, segments map directly to logical program units"],["Pure paging","Internal fragmentation inside pages","None, pages are purely mechanical"],["Segmented paging","Effectively eliminated, since every allocation unit is now a fixed size page","Preserved, the outer structure is still built from meaningful segments"]]}

This is why segmented paging shows up in real systems rather than staying a textbook curiosity. It gives the operating system meaningful, protectable units to reason about, such as marking an entire code segment read only and execute only, while giving the memory allocator itself the same fixed size, easy to manage pages that make paging so resistant to external fragmentation in the first place.
7. A Program Segments in Practice

It helps to ground all of this in what a typical running program segments actually look like. A program usually has at minimum a code segment, a data segment, a stack segment, and a heap segment, and these four behave quite differently from each other, both in size and in how that size changes while the program runs.

The code segment is fixed for the entire run of the program. It is set once when the program is loaded and never grows, since the instructions of a compiled program do not change size while it executes, and it is typically marked read only and execute only for safety. The data segment, holding global and static variables, is also largely fixed in size once the program starts, though some systems allow a small amount of controlled growth for certain kinds of static allocation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864291-872728625.png

The heap and the stack are the interesting ones, because both need to grow while the program is running, and segmentation handles this far more naturally than pure paging does. When a heap segment needs more room, the operating system can simply extend its limit in the segment table, as long as there is free space next to it, or relocate the whole segment to a bigger hole if there is not, without ever having to hunt down more scattered, discontiguous pages one at a time. The same applies to the stack, which typically grows downward as function calls nest deeper.

8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

A few misunderstandings come up often enough with segmentation that they are worth calling out directly. The first is confusing a segment limit with a page size. They sound similar but describe structurally different things: a page size is a single fixed constant shared by the entire system, decided once when the system is designed, while a segment limit is a per segment value stored in that segment own table entry, since every segment can be a different length. Saying a segment has a size of 4 kilobytes the way a page does misses the point of segmentation entirely.

The second common mistake is assuming segmentation has been completely replaced by paging in modern systems, as if it were an obsolete idea that only appears in textbooks. In reality, segmented paging hybrids are genuinely still used, giving systems the logical, permission friendly structure of segmentation combined with the fragmentation resistant allocation of paging. Pure, standalone segmentation without any paging underneath is rarer today, but the segmentation concept itself, dividing memory into meaningful, differently sized, independently protected units, is very much alive.
A third pitfall

A smaller but easy to make mistake is forgetting the limit check entirely when reasoning about address translation, and just adding base and offset without first confirming the offset is legal. In an exam or interview setting, always state the check explicitly, compare the offset to the limit first, and only compute base plus offset if that check passes. Skipping straight to the addition misses the entire protection mechanism that segmentation is built around.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: The paging versus segmentation comparison table is one of the most frequently asked memory management interview questions. Interviewers are usually listening for three things: that you can name the fragmentation type each scheme causes and explain why, that you understand a segment table entry needs both a base and a limit while a page table entry only needs a frame number, and that you know segmented paging exists as the practical middle ground most real systems reach for.
